# Frontend Frameworks {#sec-frontend-frameworks}

## Learning goals

This chapter introduces the frontend stack used in this repository: Solid, Vite, Tailwind, Kobalte, shared UI packages, and Playwright.

## Solid mental model

Solid is a fine-grained reactive UI library. It looks like React in JSX, but its reactivity model is different.

Signals are getter/setter pairs.

```tsx
import { createSignal } from "solid-js"

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = createSignal(0)

  return (
    <button onClick={() => setCount(count() + 1)}>
      Count: {count()}
    </button>
  )
}
```

The getter is a function: `count()`, not `count`.

::: {.callout-important}
## Solid signal habit

If a value comes from `createSignal`, call the getter inside reactive JSX or computations. Passing the getter function itself is a different thing.
:::

## Derived values

Use `createMemo` for derived reactive values.

```tsx
import { createMemo, createSignal } from "solid-js"

function SearchSummary() {
  const [query, setQuery] = createSignal("")
  const normalized = createMemo(() => query().trim().toLowerCase())

  return (
    <input
      value={query()}
      onInput={(event) => setQuery(event.currentTarget.value)}
      data-normalized={normalized()}
    />
  )
}
```

## Resources

`createResource` handles async data.

```tsx
import { createResource } from "solid-js"

function PackageName(props: { path: string }) {
  const [packageJson] = createResource(
    () => props.path,
    async (path) => Bun.file(`${path}/package.json`).json(),
  )

  return <span>{packageJson()?.name ?? "Loading"}</span>
}
```

In browser code, use fetch or generated clients rather than Bun APIs.

## JSX control flow

Solid uses components like `Show`, `For`, and `Switch`.

```tsx
import { For, Show } from "solid-js"

function SessionList(props: { sessions: SessionInfo[] }) {
  return (
    <Show when={props.sessions.length > 0} fallback={<p>No sessions</p>}>
      <ul>
        <For each={props.sessions}>
          {(session) => <li>{session.title ?? session.id}</li>}
        </For>
      </ul>
    </Show>
  )
}
```

## Props

Props are objects. Avoid destructuring props too early because it can break reactivity in some patterns.

```tsx
function SessionTitle(props: { session: SessionInfo }) {
  return <span>{props.session.title ?? props.session.id}</span>
}
```

## Events

Use `event.currentTarget` for typed access to the element handling the event.

```tsx
function RenameBox(props: { onRename: (name: string) => void }) {
  return (
    <input
      onInput={(event) => props.onRename(event.currentTarget.value)}
    />
  )
}
```

## Effects

`createEffect` reruns when signals read inside it change.

```tsx
import { createEffect } from "solid-js"

createEffect(() => {
  console.log("query changed", query())
})
```

Use effects for synchronization with external systems, not for ordinary derivation.

## Vite

Vite provides dev server, bundling, plugin support, and fast module reload for frontend packages.

```ts
import { defineConfig } from "vite"
import solid from "vite-plugin-solid"

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [solid()],
})
```

Package scripts:

```bash
cd packages/app
bun dev
bun build
```

## Tailwind

Tailwind is a utility-first CSS system. In this repo, it is integrated through Vite and package CSS.

```tsx
function StatusBadge(props: { status: "idle" | "running" | "failed" }) {
  return (
    <span class="rounded border px-2 py-1 text-xs">
      {props.status}
    </span>
  )
}
```

Prefer existing UI components and local class conventions over inventing a new visual language.

## Kobalte

Kobalte provides accessible Solid UI primitives. Use primitives for dialogs, menus, selects, tabs, and tooltips when local UI packages already use them.

Conceptual example:

```tsx
import { Dialog } from "@kobalte/core/dialog"

function ConfirmDialog(props: { open: boolean }) {
  return (
    <Dialog open={props.open}>
      <Dialog.Portal>
        <Dialog.Overlay />
        <Dialog.Content>
          <Dialog.Title>Confirm action</Dialog.Title>
        </Dialog.Content>
      </Dialog.Portal>
    </Dialog>
  )
}
```

## Shared UI package

`@opencode-ai/ui` exports components, hooks, contexts, styles, theme assets, icons, fonts, and v2 components. Check the package exports before adding duplicate UI.

```json
{
  "exports": {
    "./*": "./src/components/*.tsx",
    "./hooks": "./src/hooks/index.ts",
    "./theme": "./src/theme/index.ts",
    "./v2/*": "./src/v2/components/*.tsx"
  }
}
```

## Browser tests

The app package has unit, browser, and e2e scripts.

```bash
cd packages/app
bun test:unit
bun test:browser
bun test:e2e
```

Playwright drives real browser interactions.

```ts
import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test"

test("opens session list", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("/")
  await expect(page.getByText("Sessions")).toBeVisible()
})
```

## Frontend data boundaries

Frontend code should use client packages or API boundaries, not reach into server/core internals.

```ts
// Good: use client/protocol surfaces
import { Client } from "@opencode-ai/sdk"

// Bad: browser runtime depending on server/core internals
// import { SessionStore } from "@opencode-ai/core/session/store"
```

## Screen data-flow example

A frontend screen usually has four layers: route or props, client/resource call, derived view state, and user events.

```tsx
type SessionListProps = {
  readonly projectID: string
}

export function SessionList(props: SessionListProps) {
  const [sessions] = createResource(
    () => props.projectID,
    async (projectID) => client.session.list({ projectID }),
  )

  const visible = createMemo(() =>
    (sessions() ?? []).filter((session) => session.title),
  )

  return (
    <Show when={!sessions.loading} fallback={<span>Loading</span>}>
      <For each={visible()}>
        {(session) => <button>{session.title ?? session.id}</button>}
      </For>
    </Show>
  )
}
```

Testing this shape should assert user-visible behavior, not implementation details:

```ts
test("shows loaded sessions", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("/")
  await expect(page.getByRole("button", { name: "Investigate" })).toBeVisible()
})
```

Keep server data behind the client/protocol boundary, keep derived UI state in `createMemo`, and read signals/resources inside reactive scopes.

## Solid reactivity mistakes to watch for

Solid looks close enough to React that React habits can be misleading. A signal getter is a function. Reading it inside JSX, a memo, or an effect registers a reactive dependency. Passing the getter around without calling it means you are passing a function, not the current value.

```tsx
const [title, setTitle] = createSignal("Untitled")

function Header() {
  return (
    <>
      {/* Correct: call the getter to read the current value. */}
      <h1>{title()}</h1>

      {/* Correct: event handler updates the signal. */}
      <input
        value={title()}
        onInput={(event) => setTitle(event.currentTarget.value)}
      />
    </>
  )
}
```

Use `createMemo` for values derived from signals. Use `createEffect` to synchronize with something outside Solid, such as logging, storage, focus, or a subscription.

```tsx
const normalized = createMemo(() => title().trim().toLowerCase())

createEffect(() => {
  // This is a side effect, not a derived value.
  localStorage.setItem("last-title", normalized())
})
```

If you can compute a value from other reactive values, prefer a memo. If you need to make the outside world match Solid state, use an effect.

## Recap

- Solid signals are getter/setter pairs.
- Use `For`, `Show`, and other Solid control-flow components.
- Preserve prop reactivity by avoiding premature destructuring.
- Vite owns frontend dev/build behavior.
- Use shared UI and Kobalte primitives where appropriate.
- Run frontend checks from package directories.
